parsed.explanation: Section 3 proves only that V contains at most one positive value, so the exhaustive case list is V={0}, V={c}, V={0,c}. The text lists only (i) g≡0 and (ii) 'V ⊆ {0,c} with both values attainable', so the pure case V={c} (g≡c>0, 0 not attained) is indeed absent from the enumeration; the objection reads the quote correctly. However, this omitted case needs no argument at all: V={c} means g(x)=c for every x, i.e. f(x)=x+c, which is the desired conclusion, and §7 states exactly this ('the function g never takes the value 0. Together with §3 this forces g(x) ≡ c'). So the defect is one of exposition/logical bookkeeping, not of mathematical content; the necessity argument as written still yields f(x)=x+c in every case.
